---
title: "Sound 1: The Harmonic Series and Fourier"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2

A note played on a real instrument is never one frequency. It is a stack of frequencies, all at
whole-number multiples of the lowest one. That stack is the **harmonic series**, and it explains
why a violin and a flute playing the same A sound different, why the octave and the fifth sound
"pure", and how every synthesizer on the following pages works.

**How to use the page.** Every widget has a ▶ button, a picture of the wave's *shape* (an
oscilloscope) and a picture of its *spectrum* (how loud each frequency is, low on the left, high on
the right). The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume. You can play the widgets from the
computer keyboard (`a w s e d f t g y h u j k` is one octave, `z` and `x` move it), from the
on-screen keyboard, or from a MIDI keyboard. Notes go to the widget you clicked last. Click a heading
to fold a section away. Start with the volume low.

## A string vibrates in pieces

Pluck a string and it swings as a whole, but it also swings in halves, thirds, quarters and so on,
all at once. Half the length vibrates twice as fast, a third of it three times as fast. If the
whole string gives 100 Hz, the halves give 200 Hz, the thirds 300 Hz, and so on. The same happens in
the air column of a trumpet or a clarinet, and in your voice.

Each of those frequencies is a **harmonic**. The first harmonic, the whole string, is the
**fundamental**, and it's the pitch you name. The others are **overtones**. You don't hear them as
separate notes. You hear them as the *colour* (the **timbre**) of the one note.

## The series, written out

Here are the first sixteen harmonics written as notes. The number under each note is the harmonic's
number: harmonic *n* vibrates *n* times as fast as the fundamental. The number above is how far the
real harmonic is from the piano's version of that note, in **cents** (100 cents = one half step).
Choose a different fundamental and the whole series is transposed. The pattern of steps never
changes.

<div class="sk" data-w="series"></div>

Things to notice:

- **The octaves are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16.** Doubling the frequency always gives an octave.
- **The gaps shrink as you go up.** Octave, then a fifth (2 to 3), a fourth (3 to 4), a major
  third (4 to 5), a minor third (5 to 6), and then steps smaller than a minor third. The higher
  harmonics are close enough to make scales.
- **Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 are a major triad** (C, E, G over a C fundamental). The major chord is
  built into every pitched sound.
- **Harmonic 7 is about a third of a half step flat** of the piano's B♭, harmonic 11 sits almost
  exactly between F and F♯, and harmonic 13 is well sharp of A♭. Press *Harmonic, then tempered* and
  listen at those three. Piano tuning (equal temperament) moves every note slightly so that all keys
  work. The pure intervals are the harmonics.
- **The 5th harmonic is 14 cents flat** of the piano's major third. Barbershop singers and string
  quartets lean their major thirds that way, toward the harmonic.

Press *Build the tone* to hear the harmonics enter one at a time, each a little quieter than the one
before (harmonic *n* at strength 1/*n*). With all sixteen it no longer sounds like a chord. It sounds
like one buzzy note: a **sawtooth wave**.

## Fourier: every wave is a stack of sine waves

The **sine wave** is the simplest sound there is: one frequency and nothing else. It sounds pure and
a little dull, like a tuning fork or a whistle.

In 1807 Joseph Fourier showed that **any repeating wave, whatever its shape, can be built by adding
sine waves at whole-number multiples of its frequency**. Each sine wave has its own strength (and
it can be upside down). The recipe of strengths is the wave's spectrum. Going from a wave to its
recipe is the **Fourier transform**; going from the recipe back to the wave is **Fourier synthesis**.

You don't need the maths to use the idea:

- The **shape** of a wave (the oscilloscope) and its **recipe** (the spectrum) are two views of the
  same sound. Change one and the other changes.
- **Sharp corners and sudden jumps need lots of high harmonics.** Smooth, rounded shapes need few.
  Bright sounds have strong high harmonics; dark, mellow sounds don't.
- The ear mostly hears the **recipe**, not the shape. Flip a harmonic upside down and the shape
  changes a lot while the sound hardly changes.

The spectrum display under every widget on these pages is a Fourier transform done about sixty
times a second, by the browser.

## Build waves from harmonics

Each slider is one harmonic. Up is louder; below the middle line it is upside down. The numbers
under the sliders play that harmonic alone. The drawing shows the harmonics faintly and their sum in
bold. Press ▶ and move the sliders while it plays.

<div class="sk" data-w="additive"></div>

Try this:

1. Press **Sine**. One harmonic, one frequency. The spectrum shows a single spike.
2. Press **Sawtooth**: every harmonic, harmonic *n* at strength 1/*n*. Now turn **Harmonics used**
   down to 1 and slowly back up. Each added harmonic sharpens the ramp. With few harmonics the edge
   wobbles; the wobble (the **Gibbs effect**) gets narrower but never quite goes away.
3. Drag the slider for harmonic 2 to zero. The note now sounds hollow, a little like a clarinet.
4. Press **Organ**. Organ stops add harmonics 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and so on (see the
   [organ lesson](arrange-organ.qmd)): the tonebars are an additive synthesizer.

## Square, triangle, sawtooth, pulse

These four shapes are the raw material of almost every synthesizer, because each has a simple,
recognisable recipe.

| Wave | Harmonics | Strength of harmonic *n* | Sound |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sine** | 1 only | — | Pure, flute-like, no edge |
| **Sawtooth** | all | 1/*n* | Bright, buzzy, brassy and string-like |
| **Square** | odd only (1, 3, 5…) | 1/*n* | Hollow, woody, clarinet-like |
| **Triangle** | odd only | 1/*n*², alternating up and down | Soft, between sine and square |
| **Pulse** | depends on width | a pulse 1/*k* wide has no harmonics at multiples of *k* | Thin and nasal as it narrows |

Press each preset above and compare the spectrum. A **square** is a **pulse** exactly half a cycle
wide, so it's missing every 2nd harmonic. Press **Pulse 1/3** and harmonics 3, 6, 9 and 12 drop out.
**Pulse 25%** loses 4, 8, 12 and 16. The next lesson makes the pulse width move, which is **PWM**.

The triangle's harmonics fall away as 1/*n*², much faster than the square's 1/*n*, which is why
it sounds so much softer even though both have only odd harmonics.
